chapter: Los Angeles, Ellington and the recording scene
title: Who wrote "Night Train" and "Happy Go Lucky Local"
summary: Callender and Willard agree Ellington wrote it, that Jimmy Forrest took the credit, and that Ellington never sued, unlike Tizol over "Patricia".

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Because you know, there is a difference of opinion between "Night Train" and "Happy Go Lucky Local."
Well, it's the same thing!
Sure it is. But I mean, there's a difference of opinion about who wrote what.
Oh, well, Duke wrote "Happy Go Lucky Local", and Jimmy Forrest just...
Left with it. Or something.
...just lifted it. Duke didn't seem to care.
Well, Duke cared.
Oh, did he?
But Duke wasn't into suing people. He never sued anybody.
So he just let it go.
Yeah. He would, you know, make remarks about it, but...
But he never did a thing about it.
Callender (#1) - 22

No. He would just say, "This is a number we wrote," and then he would give the date, and he would sometimes say how many years before "Night Train" it was that we wrote and recorded this, and then he would play "Happy Go Lucky Local." But that's as far as he would...

Oh, it was probably ten or twelve years before "Night Train." Oh, it was an open secret. Everybody knew Duke wrote it. But Jimmy Forrest recorded it and put his name on it, and... Well, he got the credit for "Night Train." But everybody knows that it was "Happy Go Lucky Local" that knew anything about Duke Ellington.

How come when Basie played it, when Jimmy Forrest was in Basie's band, at the end of Jimmy Forrest's solo Basie would always say, "And the composer of 'Night Train,'" and Jimmy Forrest would take ten bows.
Well, everybody knew it. I guess it got to be a joke actually. Because Jimmy Forrest got away with it.
Yes, he did.
Well, I guess Duke was a bigger man than a lot of people realize, in a lot of ways. Because he didn't have to let it go. He just said, "What the hell. It can't hurt me that much."
Whereas on the other hand, I think, Juan Tizol sued Perez Prado, when Perez Prado got a hit with
Callender (#1) - 23
"Patricia", which Juan said was his "Perdido" at a different tempo.
That's true. It was.
But Duke wouldn't sue.
